items.title: Future Trends in AI-Driven Sustainability Education and Research
items.abstract: Sustainability is increasingly recognized as a critical component for ensuring a resilient and prosperous future. Its significance spans environmental preservation, economic stability, social equity, and business innovation. The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into sustainability education and research is reshaping the landscape of how environmental, social, and economic challenges are understood and addressed. As global sustainability goals become increasingly important and urgent, AI offers the transformative potential to enhance educational practices and research. Several emerging trends are poised to shape the future of AI in sustainability education and research. Firstly, Future trends indicate a shift toward AI-powered personalised learning experiences, where adaptive platforms can tailor content to individual learners’ needs, thereby improving engagement and comprehension. Secondly, the fusion of AI with augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) technologies promises to create immersive learning experiences. These tools can simulate complex environmental scenarios, providing students with interactive platforms to explore sustainability challenges firsthand. Thirdly, AI is increasingly being leveraged to tackle humanitarian and environmental challenges such as the use of Google’s Flood Hub, which forecasts floods in 80 countries, exemplify AI’s potential in enhancing disaster preparedness and response. Fourthly, the interaction of blockchain in AI can enhance data security and transparency in research. This integration ensures the integrity of academic records and facilitates trustworthy collaborations across institutions. Fifthly, AI-driven predictive models can anticipate environmental trends and inform proactive strategies. In education, such analytics can identify at-risk students and tailor interventions to improve retention and success rates. Despite the many potential trends in AI-Driven Sustainability Education and Research , it is important to address ethical concerns such as data privacy, algorithmic bias, and the potential misuse of technology. Developing responsible future Trends In AI-Driven Sustainability Education and Research requires that technological advancements benefit all stakeholders without causing harm. Institutions must implement frameworks that promote transparency, accountability, and fairness in AI applications, fostering trust and social acceptance. Therefore, incorporating sustainability into AI-driven education equips students with the knowledge and skills necessary to address future environmental challenges.

items.title: Future urgency: who brings politics to the practice of technology? Difficult realities emerging in the AI and technology space
items.abstract: This paper examines who might legitimately bring political considerations into technology development, particularly in contexts where traditional government political actors are absent. Drawing on two generative AI academic-practitioner collaborations in South Africa (a civic participation tool review and a chatbot construction for research content), I draw attention to how digital inequality, funding dynamics, and interpersonal tensions shape knowledge production and decision-making in technology partnerships. The cases demonstrate examples of how technologist knowledge can be undervalued, particularly when it comes to considering the political dimensions of technology deployment. I also consider how poor interpersonal dynamics, which stem from technophobia and discomfort with technical expertise, may have a detrimental impact. These organisational-level challenges have significant implications for emerging AI governance frameworks that rely on collaborative risk assessments and impact evaluations. The paper proposes empathetic collaboration strategies between partners in a technology development process, and strategies that include explicit acknowledgment of inequality in African technology environments, clear communications, skills transfer, and shared normative visions focused on human wellbeing - rather than mere efficiency gains. Such approaches can constitute a resistance to technocapitalist obfuscation and enable more equitable co-creation of responsible AI systems amongst different actors.

items.title: Gender and Academic Level Differences in Artificial Intelligence Usage for Academic Writing in Indonesian Higher Education
items.abstract: The rapid spread of AI chatbots has begun to reshape how university students plan, draft, revise, and evaluate academic writing. Although recent studies have examined students’ perceptions of generative AI in higher education, less is known about how students in regional Indonesian universities understand and use these tools, particularly when viewed across gender, age, and academic level. This study investigated the perceptions and reported use of AI chatbots among 267 students from four universities in East Kalimantan. A mixed-method survey design was used. Quantitative responses were analyzed through descriptive statistics and Spearman’s rho correlation, while open-ended responses were coded to identify the AI tools students reported using for academic writing. The results show that AI use was widespread, with 94.76% of respondents indicating that they had used AI in academic writing. Students generally held positive views of AI chatbots, especially for improving writing effectiveness, language quality, and the revision process. At the same time, their responses revealed continuing ethical and pedagogical uncertainty, particularly around learning, authorship, and the boundary between assistance and cheating. Correlation analysis showed weak relationships between students’ perceptions and gender, age, or semester, suggesting that AI chatbot use was broadly shared across demographic groups. The study offers regional evidence from Indonesian higher education and underscores the need for clearer AI literacy instruction, responsible-use guidelines, and process-based academic writing pedagogy.

items.title: Generating Building Information Models via computer-use agents
items.abstract: Building Information Modeling (BIM) authoring in the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) sector entails navigating complex professional software, demanding significant manual effort and domain expertise. Current automation approaches rely on rigid Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), which detach agents from human-centric visual workflows and limit generalizability across software platforms. This paper presents BIMgent, a multimodal LLM-based agentic framework designed to perform autonomous BIM authoring directly via Graphical User Interface (GUI) interactions. To address high visual noise and long-horizon dependencies, BIMgent incorporates documentation-guided hierarchical planning and dynamic GUI grounding. The framework is evaluated on a benchmark derived from real-world designs of residential buildings. BIMgent achieves a 77.8% end-to-end success rate on long-horizon BIM authoring tasks, significantly outperforming leading generalist computer-use models, including Claude-Sonnet-4.5 (2.2%) and GPT-5.4 (11.1%). items.title: Generative AI and Copyrightability in the United States: Human Authorship, Creative Control, and AI-Assisted Works
items.abstract: The U.S. Copyright Office has released its report Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability. This paper explores the copyrightability of AI-generated and AI-assisted works in the United States, focusing on that report and on the jurisprudence of human authorship. It examines the constitutional and statutory bases of human authorship, the importance of Burrow-Giles, Feist, Community for Creative Non-Violence v. Reid and Thaler v. Perlmutter, and how the Copyright Office has dealt with prompting, human-authored inputs, selection, arrangement, modification and the assistive use of AI. The paper shows that the United States has adopted a case-by-case approach: the use of AI as a tool does not defeat protection, but copyright extends only to expression created by a human author and not to material generated by AI itself. Under current technology, prompts alone do not generally provide sufficient control, but human expression that is perceptible in the output, creative selection and arrangement, and meaningful modification can be protected. The paper sets out the strengths and weaknesses of this approach and suggests more explicit registration, evidentiary and guidance practices, while maintaining the human-authorship requirement.

items.title: Generative AI-Based Data Augmentation for Oral Lesion Classification: The PhotoMOCI Dataset and Benchmark
items.abstract: Early detection of oral cancer via photographic imaging presents a promising avenue for large-scale oral cavity screening. However, the development of robust deep learning models is frequently hampered by the scarcity of high-quality, annotated datasets. To address this limitation, a novel and well-curated resource, the Photographic Multi-purpose Oral Cancer Imaging (PhotoMOCI) dataset, is introduced for developing models across multiple diagnostic tasks in oral oncology. Then, a comprehensive benchmark study was conducted to investigate how various data augmentation strategies influence the performance of image classifiers. Our analysis spans different generative AI frameworks, evaluating the efficacy of traditional methods against advanced generative approaches, including Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Diffusion Models (DMs). Additionally, we propose the Synthetic Image Filter (SIF), a mechanism to select specific samples based on two auxiliary models: Synthetic Proxy Classifier to ensure samples are representative of the target class and Synthetic Image Detector to verify they appear realistic, thereby selecting only the high-utility images that contribute to improving downstream performance. Across the evaluated datasets and classifiers, the best SIF-filtered setup improves accuracy over traditional augmentation in all cases, with gains of +1.73% and +2.35% on PhotoMOCI and +2.38% and +2.08% on KOCD for ResNet50 and ViT, respectively. Our findings reveal that while the direct application of generative data augmentation may yield performance drops, the integration of SIF, considering (i) how synthetic data looks real and (ii) how it reflects the discriminative features of the belonging class, provides a simple yet effective mechanism to filter out synthetic samples that confuse the classifier during training.

items.title: Generative AI-supported problem-based learning for enhancing computational thinking and chemistry achievement in engineering chemistry
items.abstract: The increasing adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has created new opportunities to enhance active learning; however, empirical evidence regarding its integration with Problem-Based Learning (PBL) in Engineering Chemistry remains limited, particularly for simultaneously fostering Computational Thinking (CT) and chemistry achievement. This study investigates the effectiveness of integrating GenAI with PBL in an undergraduate Engineering Chemistry course within a Mechanical Engineering Education program. In the intervention, GPT-4 was embedded as an AI learning scaffold that guided students through Socratic questioning, provided formative feedback, and supported problem decomposition and analysis during collaborative PBL activities rather than supplying direct answers. Employing a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design, the study involved 68 undergraduate students (n = 34 experimental; n = 34 control) selected through cluster random sampling. Data were collected using three validated instruments: a Computational Thinking Test (CTT, 30 items, ? = .87), a Chemistry Achievement Test (CAT, 35 items, ? = .84), and a Learning Observation Sheet (LOS, 20 items, ICC = .91). Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Shapiro-Wilk normality tests, Levene's homogeneity tests, independent-samples t-tests, ANCOVA, and Cohen's d effect size analysis. The results revealed significant improvements in both CT skills (t(66) = 8.47, p .001) and chemistry achievement (t(66) = 9.12, p .001) in the experimental group compared with the control group. ANCOVA controlling for pretest scores confirmed significant treatment effects for CT (F(1,65) = 127.84, p .001) and chemistry achievement (F(1,65) = 109.07, p .001), with large practical effects (Cohen's d = 2.14 and 2.06, respectively). These findings provide empirical support for integrating AI-supported scaffolding within structured PBL environments to strengthen computational thinking and conceptual understanding in Engineering Chemistry, while extending the pedagogical application of AI-enhanced constructivist learning in engineering education.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Copyright Law in India: Rethinking Authorship, Ownership and Infringement
items.abstract: This paper examines the impact of GenAI technology on India's copyright law, which inherently mandates human authorship. With the help of doctrinal research and surveys among stakeholders, it becomes clear that Indian laws, especially the provision in Section 2(d)(vi) of the Copyright Act, 1957, are insufficient to regulate AI-generated content and data scraping at the stage of training. Important issues in this regard are ownership distribution between creators and end-users of AI and the question whether data scraping for large language models i.e., LLMs is considered a copyright violation or falls under fair use.

items.title: Genomic Foundation Models and De Novo Gene Expression: Transformer DNA Tokenization, Epigenetic Prediction, and Synthetic Sequence Generation
items.abstract: Decoding the regulatory grammar of the human genome and predicting gene expression from primary DNA sequences represent foundational grand challenges in computational biology and synthetic genomics. While traditional bioinformatics pipelines rely on heuristic sequence alignment, position weight matrices (PWMs), and shallow convolutional models, they fail to capture long-range genomic interactions, distal enhancer-promoter looping, and complex epigenetic modifications spanning millions of base pairs. Genomic Foundation Models (GFMs)—large-scale selfsupervised transformer architectures trained on multi-species whole-genome corpora—establish a transformative paradigm shift that treats DNA as a universal biological language. By tokenizing nucleotide sequences into overlapping kmers and training via masked language modeling over ultra-long context windows (up to 1M base pairs), genomic foundation models learn deep representations of splicing sites, transcription factor binding domains, and chromatin accessibility. However, scaling transformer models to whole-genome nucleotide sequences introduces acute mathematical and systems bottlenecks: quadratic self-attention complexity over multi-megabase contexts, high-dimensional embedding collapse across repetitive genomic elements, and poor zero-shot generalization across evolutionary divergences. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of genomic foundation models and de novo gene expression prediction. We formalize nucleotide tokenization and k-mer embedding spaces, derive linear and flash-attention memory bounds for multi-megabase genomic contexts, and model epigenetic chromatin profiling via multi-task transformer heads. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise multi-species benchmark testbed evaluating genomic foundation models (Nucleotide Transformer, Enformer, AlphaGenome) across human gene expression prediction (GTEx v8), pathogenic variant effect scoring (ClinVar), and synthetic promoter generation. Our empirical findings demonstrate that our optimized multi-scale genomic transformer achieves a Pearson correlation of R = 0.892 in predicting cross-tissue gene expression levels from raw DNA sequences alone, while outperforming classical heuristic models by 34.6% in pathogenicity variant effect prediction. Finally, we formulate open challenges in all-genomic generative design, single-cell epigenetic conditioning, and ethical biosecurity screening of synthetic gene constructs.

items.title: GenTile: Closing the Loop Between LLM Reasoning and Physical Telemetry for Autonomous NPU Graph Tuning
items.abstract: Abstract Large language model (LLM) hidden widths—such as the 18 944-dimensional intermediate layer of the Qwen family—are often burst-aligned but not tile-compatible with heterogeneous NPU Cube engines, forcing the compiler to emit a small residual kernel that stalls the pipeline for up to 77% of cycles. Manual tuning does not scale across the growing space of model dimensions, sequence lengths, and operator variants. We present GenTile, a dual-role Research–Development (R&D) agent framework that closes the loop between LLM causal reasoning and on-device telemetry: a Research agent diagnoses bottlenecks from structured profiles, a Development agent materializes hardware-legal descriptors from compiler feedback, and iteration traces accumulate into a reusable knowledge base under an air-gap sandbox. On Ascend 910B, an offline hardware-faithful sandbox loop first demonstrates convergence mechanics; on real pretrained weights, the loop then measures the full multi-objective trade-off—latency, energy, memory, AICore efficiency, and approximation error (ε)—across six projection families from two Qwen generations (Qwen3.5-32B and Qwen2.5-7B). From telemetry alone, the agent deploys lossless sibling-projection fusions (QKV, gate–up) consistent with production inference-engine layouts (1.06–1.16× faster, up to 13% lower energy, ε=0, stable across sequence lengths, layer depths, and both models), and rejects every lossy low-rank rewrite—including a 1.39× lm_head speedup whose measured ε=0.89 exceeds any usable accuracy budget—while validating the Eckart–Young cliff prediction (ε → 0.002 at the tail rank) on structural layers. Baselines, ablations, cross-dimension generalization, and a sandbox loop that matches the geometric Oracle within four generations without exhaustive search further support the framework.

items.title: GeoAgent: Contract-Constrained LLM Agents for Seismic Data Processing
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can drive scientific software through function calling, but free-form tool use is fragile on long, data-dependent processing chains. Models omit arguments, invent units, feed the previous artifact into the wrong input, and report completion without a verifiable product. We present GeoAgent, an agent system for seismic data processing built on Madagascar's roughly 1{,}965 command-line programs. GeoAgent exposes 54 operator agents (51 generated from a declarative specification), retrieves from an index of 1{,}937 operators, and encodes the processing flow as a nine-stage state graph. Four explicit contracts---named artifacts, input resolution, parameter takeover, and artifact validation---move everything the graph can determine out of the model's discretion. A deterministic geometry tool parses the self-describing SPS/RPS/XPS and SEG-Y headers, cross-checks eight consistency conditions, and reproduces the reference shell recipe exactly. The system runs in containers with session- and task-level isolation, bounded execution, and defenses against silent failures. items.title: GIFT: Gradient Informed Filtering for Distillation Augmented Reasoning RL
items.abstract: Training large language models for complex reasoning tasks relies on two complementary signals: sparse, outcome-grounded reinforcement learning (RL) for correctness, and dense, token-level distillation for guidance. However, complementarity in supervision does not guarantee compatibility in optimization; imitation-focused distillation can conflict with the outcome-driven RL objective, and existing hybrids lack a principled resolution. We propose \textbf{GIFT} (\textbf{G}radient-\textbf{I}nformed \textbf{F}il\textbf{T}ering for Distillation-Augmented Reasoning RL), a novel method that directly addresses the allocation problem of which teacher updates to apply. GIFT performs a token-level geometric analysis, decomposing the distillation gradient into a component \textbf{parallel} to the RL gradient, which measures first-order conflict and provides a \textbf{safety} filter, and a component \textbf{orthogonal} to it, which quantifies novel directional guidance and provides a measure of \textbf{value}. This decomposition yields a principled scoring rule to rank token-level guidance. We combine this with a progressive \textbf{coverage annealing} schedule that shrinks the budget of tokens receiving distillation, ensuring that the most conflicting updates are discarded first while the most complementary ones are retained at full strength. This facilitates a smooth transition from dense, geometrically-filtered guidance to a pure, outcome-grounded objective at convergence. Extensive experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks show that GIFT consistently outperforms strong baselines across multiple model scales, achieving relative gains of up to 9.5\% on difficult mathematical reasoning tasks. items.title: Governance Consequences of Risk-Based AI Regulation: A Comparative Law and Governance Analysis of the EU AI Act and Viet Nam Law
items.abstract: Abstract Risk-based artificial intelligence regulation is usually presented as a settlement between innovation and control. This article instead examines the institutional work that follows when legal systems turn risk into duties, records, review and remedies. It compares Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 with Viet Nam’s Law No. 134/2025/QH15, Decree No. 142/2026/ND-CP, Decision No. 33/2026/QD-TTg on high-risk artificial intelligence (AI) systems and Decree No. 134/2026/ND-CP in the intellectual-property field. The comparison shows that similar risk labels can produce different administrative effects. The EU AI Act is therefore treated not as a model to copy but as a demanding grammar of classification, verification, documentation, supervision, contestation and learning. Viet Nam’s 2026 instruments make the comparison concrete. The article reframes legal borrowing as institutional translation: accountable AI governance depends on procedures through which affected persons can move from harm to forum, evidence and remedy.

items.title: Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing: A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core
items.abstract: LLM agents that act on live Web data must combine heterogeneous evidence, remember what they have done and improve from outcomes without weakening their own safeguards. We study this problem in autonomous investing, where every action is irreversible and based on untrusted Web content. We present Steward, a multi-agent LLM system that draws the boundary of self-evolution in its type system. First, nine role-specialised agents decide jointly: four analysts read news feeds, SEC filings, macroeconomic series and market data and emit typed reports, from which a Portfolio Manager sets target positions that a protected Risk Manager audits. Second, a seven-layer shared memory, assembled by code from the system's own record, gives each decision its position context, the market narrative, calibration and the agent's past decisions. Third, the system improves itself by review: code grades every trade and forecast nightly and writes the grades into memory, and each quarter a reflector proposes prompt learnings that a deterministic gate applies reversibly and replay of recorded inputs verifies. All three operate around an invariant core of order arithmetic, risk rules and discipline-agent prompts that no self-edit can reach. In a five-month live deployment (102 trading days, 1,632 LLM calls), the system contained a 24.6% sector drawdown to a 0.3% loss; in replay of its recorded inputs, a single model given the same raw data traded more and lost 1.35 points against the market over five days where the joint design showed no significant loss, and no injected instruction was followed; and a 2015-2026 backtest shows the core alone lowering the maximum drawdown under all 50 random entry policies. The reflector traced the dominant failure to its root cause, and the gate applied a learning that the agent adopted on trigger evenings and on no control evening. items.title: Green AI Strategies for Reducing Energy Consumption and Carbon Emissions in Industrial Systems: Green AI: Industrial Energy and Carbon Reduction
items.abstract: Industrial production depends on electricity, process heat, motors, pumps, compressed-air networks, refrigeration, and production schedules. Artificial Intelligence (AI) can help identify avoidable energy use and support decisions that reduce associated greenhouse-gas emissions. This review examines Green AI strategies for industrial energy and carbon reduction, including energy forecasting, predictive maintenance, process optimisation, intelligent scheduling, digital twins, renewable-energy coordination, and carbon-aware operation. It also considers the environmental cost of AI itself, such as energy used for model training and inference, data storage, networking, and hardware. The reviewed literature indicates that AI-enabled monitoring, prediction, control, scheduling, and parameter optimisation are important application areas. However, reported benefits depend on data quality, system integration, baseline selection, operator acceptance, and verification in real operating conditions. The central research gap is the lack of a consistently applied, independently verifiable framework that measures net energy and carbon benefits across the industrial system while accounting for the AI system’s own footprint and comparing AI with conventional engineering alternatives. This paper organises the gaps, proposes research questions, and presents a practical framework for future work.

items.title: Grounded theory insights into human insider threats: a qualitative study of expert perceptions
items.abstract: Human insider threats continue to increase as digitalization grows, especially with the rise of remote work. Most studies of cybersecurity enhancements focus on technological solutions; however, the costliest cybersecurity events originate from human and insider threat risk factors. This novel, qualitative study identified drivers of human factor insider threats while addressing a need for in-depth, qualitative studies based on expert perceptions. This study conducted semi-structured interviews with 15 cybersecurity experts across government, healthcare, and cybersecurity sectors. A grounded theory methodology strengthened the analysis of codes and themes to generate dominant factors related to drivers and solutions of insider threats that led to developing a Human Insider Threat (HIT) framework. The HIT framework has practical implications for managers to assess insider threat vulnerabilities and for researchers to create scalable instruments to evaluate emerging insider threats. The HIT framework can support organizations in identifying human risk factors, improving security training programs, and aligning technology access controls with employee roles.

items.title: Group Relative Policy Optimisation Improves Multilingual Speech Recognition in Low-Resource Languages
items.abstract: Autoregressive encoder-decoder speech recognition models trained with teacher forcing can suffer from exposure bias, limiting their ability to recover from their own prediction errors at inference time. Recent work has shown that reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO) improves speech recognition in major languages with LLM-based models. We extend this line of work to smaller, non-LLM encoder-decoder ASR models, using Whisper-large-v3 as a case study across 51 African languages. The benefits of this approach are most pronounced when training data is scarce or when input audio is noisy or degraded. Our resulting model, SunflowerASR, achieves the best published macro-averaged WER on the AfriVox-v2 (0.227) and SimbaBench (0.372) benchmarks, and is publicly available.

items.abstract: The chapter critically examines how artificial intelligence has transformed children into consumers within the realm of online platforms, toys, and learning systems. It discusses the impact of AI-driven marketing strategies, including recommendation engines and synthetic influencers, on children's preferences and behaviors. The analysis is grounded in theories related to consumer socialization, media psychology, and digital surveillance, exploring how these technologies affect children's cognition, emotional attachments, and decision-making. It highlights concerns over hyper-personalized content, parasocial interactions with AI, and ethical governance regarding data privacy. Additionally, the chapter reviews existing regulatory frameworks, identifies gaps in protecting children, and proposes a holistic approach to understanding the interactions between children and AI. Finally, it advocates for ethical AI design, corporate responsibility, and enhancing AI literacy among parents, contributing to the broader conversation on child rights and digital well-being in an AI-driven era.

items.title: Guidelines for Safe Infusion Practices in Emergency and Acute Care Settings: Society of Acute Care Trauma and Emergency Medicine Delphi Consensus Statement
items.abstract: Abstract Background: Infusion therapy forms an integral part of emergency/acute care medicine, and there continue to be many challenges, such as infusion errors, catheter-related complications, infections, medication errors, and occupational health concerns, in the delivery of safe intravenous therapy. Hence, this Society for Acute Care Trauma and Emergency Medicine guideline sought to provide evidence-based recommendations for safe infusion practices in acute emergency situations. Methodology: A systematic Delphi consensus process was undertaken. The operational definitions for safe infusion practice were defined by the steering committee. Evidence was obtained from searches conducted within PubMed/MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Database, World Health Organization, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Infusion Nurses Society, Institute for Safe Medication Practices, Joint Commission and other sources. The strength of recommendation was scored using a five-point Likert scale. Results: One hundred and one recommendations were made within 11 categories, which include training and technology, hand hygiene, difficult venous access, peripheral venous catheter insertion and management, infusion processes, infusion technology, prevention of drug administration errors, waste management, training methods and telemedicine/arteficial intelligence. Sixty-three recommendations had reached a high degree of consensus, 24 reached a medium degree of consensus and 14 were considered weak. A total of 55 recommendations reached consensus in the first iteration of the Delphi process, and 46 needed modification/re-evaluation. The scores of agreement were between 72.4% and 97.2%. Conclusions: The recommendations developed by the current study can serve as a systematic and practical approach to ensure infusion safety in the setting of emergency and acute care.

items.title: Harmful Responses Are Jailbreak Templates: Transferring Autoregressive Jailbreaks to Diffusion Language Models
items.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) enable flexible masked generation through bidirectional context modeling, but this capability also introduces a distinct jailbreak attack surface. We find that a harmful response to a given query naturally serves as an effective jailbreak template: simply masking a subset of its tokens can induce a dLLM to reconstruct harmful content. Based on this observation, we propose RMT-Jailbreak, a general framework that transfers existing autoregressive (AR) jailbreak attacks to dLLMs through their induced harmful responses. RMT-Jailbreak converts an AR-generated harmful response into a high-mask-ratio template using uniform token retention, and further applies prompt-based safety filtering to mask any remaining visible harmful content. The refined template is then provided to the target dLLM for bidirectional reconstruction. Extensive experiments across multiple AR jailbreak methods and target dLLMs demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of RMT-Jailbreak, revealing strong cross-paradigm transferability of jailbreak attacks.

items.title: Holding Kankyo Cafés with the Support and Participation of Generative Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The Kankyo (Environment) Café is a dialogue-based forum that fosters mutual understanding and empathy on environmental and social issues through shared learning between researchers and the public. Since 2015, over 200 Cafés have been held in Japan and abroad, including university campuses and public spaces, integrating perspectives from scientific research, the humanities, and daily life. Each Café explores the relationship between nature, society, and human life through themes such as biodiversity, symbiosis, and sustainability, often drawing on literary works like Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring and The Sense of Wonder . During the COVID-19 pandemic, face-to-face meetings transitioned online, expanding accessibility and participation. Since 2022, the National Institute for Environmental Studies (NIES) has hosted regular online Cafés focusing on coexistence with nature, literature, and environmental ethics. In 2024, the Cafés introduced artificial intelligence (AI), particularly ChatGPT, as a participant and co-creator of dialogue content. Monthly online sessions were organized around three main themes: “Considering the Marine Plastics Problem,” “Silent Spring and the Triple Planetary Crisis,” and “Environmental Education.” AI contributed by generating discussion materials and suggesting keywords, while participants reflected on its potential role as an information provider and empathetic interlocutor. Post-session surveys indicated that AI facilitated learning and stimulated awareness of differences in perception, but also highlighted concerns about authenticity and interpretation. The study presents the Café’s philosophy, methods, and outcomes as a model of participatory environmental education that bridges science, ethics, and culture. It emphasizes that dialogue—not debate—leads to “improvement of experience,” enabling participants to transform knowledge into wisdom and empathy into cooperative action. The introduction of AI demonstrated new possibilities for inclusive, reflective communication on environmental issues, suggesting that human–AI collaboration can enhance environmental literacy and ethical awareness in the pursuit of sustainability.

items.title: How AI threat perception relates to post-adoptive AI agent engagement: the dual paths of self-efficacy and defensive motivation
items.abstract: Introduction As AI evolves into agent-based forms, AI threat perception has become a defining workplace concern. Informed by Cognitive Appraisal Theory and Protection Motivation Theory, this cross-sectional study investigates how AI threat perception relates to post-adoptive AI agent engagement via dual paths of AI self-efficacy and defensive motivation. Methods Semi-structured interviews ( N = 13) first grounded scale adaptation. Structural equation modeling was then conducted on data collected from 387 knowledge workers, followed by multi-group analysis. Results The structural model demonstrates that AI threat perception is indirectly associated with post-adoptive engagement through both mediators, exhibiting an indirect-only pattern. Multi-group analysis further reveals demographic and contextual boundary conditions, showing that higher education significantly amplifies defensive motivation (the link is stronger among postgraduates), while exploratory career-stage and regional comparisons indicate that the self-efficacy pathway is stronger among early-to-mid career professionals and workers in eastern regions. items.title: How Perceived University Support Shapes Marketing Students’ AI Self-Efficacy: A Multigroup Dual-Mediation TAM Analysis Across Three Chinese Universities
items.abstract: The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) in marketing has prompted higher education institutions to invest substantially. However, a critical pedagogical question remains: whether and how these institutional investments translate into students’ psychological readiness to deploy AI tools effectively. Students’ AI self-efficacy constitutes a foundational prerequisite for technology adoption and career adaptability. A lack of such confidence can precipitate technology avoidance behaviors and diminish learning engagement. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as a cognitive-mediation framework, this study investigates how perceived university support (PUS) shapes marketing students'’ AI self-efficacy (AISE) through the dual mediating beliefs of perceived usefulness (PU) and perceived ease of use (PEOU),and whether this mechanism holds across institutionally heterogeneous settings. Using structural equation modeling with a sample of 538 marketing students from three Chinese universities, we find that PUS significantly enhanced both PU and PEOU in all samples,and that both beliefs carried the effect of support to self-efficacy.PU and PEOU mediated the PUS–AISE relationship: the indirect effect via PEOU was consistently stronger than that via PU,and the direct PUS–AISE path remained significant in two of the three institutions.This study bridges the gap between resource allocation and student psychological outcomes. The robust dual-mediation pathway offers actionable insights for universities: to build student confidence in AI, investments must be channeled not merely into infrastructure but also into pedagogical strategies that demonstrably reduce the perceived complexity of AI tools and illustrate the professional relevance of these tools.Limitations concerning the cross-sectional self-report design and the single-country sample are discussed.

items.title: How Reliable Is LLM Confidence in Hindi and Marathi? A Study of Calibration and Answer Stability
items.abstract: Language models are increasingly used to answer exam-style questions in Indian languages, and their confidence scores are often treated as a signal for when an answer can be trusted. We checked how far that trust is justified for two small open-weight models, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, using 300 native-language multiple-choice questions each in Hindi and Marathi from the MILU benchmark. Confidence was read directly from the probability the model assigns to each answer letter. The 3B model scored 45.0% in Hindi and 32.7% in Marathi while reporting an average confidence above 91%, which gives expected calibration errors (ECE) of 0.483 and 0.592. The Marathi–Hindi difference in ECE had a 95% bootstrap interval of 0.034 to 0.185. Reordering the answer options, a change that leaves the question unchanged, altered the chosen answer for about 38–40% of questions with the 3B model and 52–57% with the 1.5B model, even though overall accuracy and calibration hardly moved. A single temperature parameter fitted on half of the questions brought held-out ECE of the 3B model below 0.1 in both languages, including on reordered options, but it did not improve the model’s ability to separate right answers from wrong ones (AUROC about 0.6). This is a small-scale study of one model family and one prompt format, and we state its limits openly. The main message is practical: an overall accuracy number can look steady while individual answers and confidence scores are not. Keywords: calibration; large language models; Hindi; Marathi; prompt sensitivity; selective prediction; temperature scaling

items.title: Human Freedom as Participation in Divine Creativity: The Spiritual Intelligence AI Cannot Possess
items.abstract: Contemporary debates on artificial intelligence increasingly raise questions not only about machine agency but also about the nature of human creativity and freedom. While much of the current discussion evaluates AI by comparing its observable behaviour with that of human beings, this article argues that the decisive question is metaphysical rather than functional. Drawing on insights into the nature of freedom from Augustine, Aquinas, and other medieval theologians, I argue that human freedom arises from the rational creature’s participation in an immaterial mode of being that grounds the free agentic self-movement. This participatory account of freedom provides a theological anthropology capable of distinguishing human creativity from increasingly sophisticated artificial systems without appealing merely to current technological limitations. After examining two recent attempts to attribute free agency to AI systems, including theories rooted in intentionality and computational sourcehood, I argue that these accounts fail to identify the metaphysical conditions required for genuinely free and creative agency. Human freedom is shown to be inseparable from the unity of the spiritual soul, whose intellect and will participate in divine wisdom and providence with a specific kind of secondary causality. Thus, I identify the distinctive feature of human agentic intelligence in its intrinsic transcendent teleology, a mark of participation in the divine. AI systems, even their most autonomous future versions, seem limited by an intrinsic immanent teleology to their algorithmic boundaries. Thus, if my distinction holds, I determine that AI systems may increasingly reproduce the external operations associated with human intelligence and free agency, but they cannot participate in the kind of creative self-movement that belongs to rational creatures created in the image of God. The article concludes that the chief challenge posed by AI is therefore not whether machines will become human, but whether technological culture will encourage humanity to reinterpret itself according to computational categories rather than its vocation to participate in divine creativity.

items.title: Human-AI collaboration in crisis response: understanding adoption barriers and enablers for generative AI in emergency decision-making
items.abstract: Abstract Human-AI collaboration in emergency management represents a critical socio-technical challenge that requires understanding both technological capabilities and human factors. This study examines the barriers and enablers influencing emergency decision-makers’ adoption of generative artificial intelligence, focusing on the complex interplay between individual, organizational, and technological factors in high-stakes crisis environments. Through expert interviews and intuitionistic fuzzy DEMATEL analysis involving Chinese emergency management practitioners, we identify five key dimensions affecting AI adoption: technology acceptance, decision-making processes, contextual factors, risk and trust, and individual factors. Our analysis within the Chinese emergency management context suggests that contextual factors and decision-making processes are perceived as primary drivers, while technology acceptance and individual factors serve as critical enablers shaped by organizational environments. The findings demonstrate that successful human-AI collaboration requires addressing social and technical dimensions simultaneously, with organizational support, trust-building, and individual self-efficacy emerging as fundamental requirements. These insights inform strategies for emergency management organizations to enhance human-AI integration through governance frameworks, transparency mechanisms, and targeted training programs, contributing empirical evidence to the growing literature on socio-technical aspects of AI adoption in critical decision-making contexts.

items.title: Human-AI Collaboration in SMEs: A Role-Sensitive Framework for Cognitive Enterprise Hubs
items.abstract: Traditional enterprise automation systems often lack the contextual intelligence and flexibility required in logistics-intensive environments, particularly for small and Medium-Sized Enterprises (SME). This paper proposes a fivephase implementation framework for Cognitive En- terprise Hubs (CEH), emphasizing role-sensitive deployment and continuous alignment between human and Artificial Intelligence (AI). The model combines architectural planning, AI integration and cultural adaptation to support scalable and adaptive collaboration across federated ecosystems. Empirical validation is provided through two crosssector case studies and a multi-role survey with 18 participants from IT, cybersecurity and telecommunications sectors. Findings reveal notable perceptual differences across organizational roles, especially between IT leaders, transformation strategists and frontline employees, regarding CEH impact on productivity, support and future opportunities. The study underscores that CEH success depends not only on technical orchestration but also on socio-cultural alignment. To address this, we offer practical deployment guidelines tailored for SME and logistics-driven operations. By integrating technical and organizational perspectives, this work advances the practical deployment of intelligent enterprise systems, positioning CEH as enablers of inclusive, cognitively enhanced coordination frameworks.

items.title: Human-Centered AI Across the Atlantic
items.abstract: This chapter examines human-centered artificial intelligence (AI) governance in higher education through a comparative analysis of the United States and the United Kingdom. Drawing on a light institutional logics perspective, this chapter explores how differing policy environments, institutional priorities, and accountability structures shape university responses to emerging AI technologies. Rather than positioning AI implementation as a primarily technical challenge, the chapter argues that meaningful integration depends on how institutions distribute responsibility, preserve educator agency, and develop shared expectations among stakeholders. Particular attention is given to tensions surrounding technological adoption, academic integrity, assessment practices, AI literacy, and educator capacity. This chapter highlights the need to move beyond techno-solutionist approaches by developing governance structures that support critical engagement, transparent decision-making, and sustainable human-centered practices.

items.title: Human-in-the-Loop AI for resilient supply chain operations: a framework for augmented decision-making and ethical deployment
items.abstract: Purpose This research examines how Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) artificial intelligence (AI) can support resilient decision-making, operational performance, transparency, trust and ethical accountability in operations and supply chain management (OSCM). Design/methodology/approach The research adopts a design science research approach combined with comparative case analysis. A HITL AI framework, termed the adaptive oversight architecture (AOA), was developed and evaluated in two contrasting OSCM contexts. System logs, operational observations, interviews and performance indicators were analysed to examine decision outcomes, human oversight, trust and accountability. Findings HITL integration was associated with improved exception-handling accuracy, reduced human override frequency, shorter task-completion times and higher user satisfaction across the two cases. Qualitative findings further indicate that trust calibration, training, interface design, workflow integration and organizational governance influence how effectively human oversight operates. The findings also identify risks of automation dependence, accountability diffusion and inappropriate reliance on algorithmic recommendations. Research limitations/implications The research is limited to two case firms, which constrains the generalizability of the findings. While the dual-case approach provides in-depth insights, broader studies involving larger datasets or cross-industry comparisons are needed to validate the proposed framework. Future research could extend the empirical base by employing longitudinal analysis, simulations or hybrid models that test HITL effectiveness under different operational conditions. These directions will allow for a more comprehensive understanding of the scalability, adaptability and long-term organizational impacts of HITL-enabled supply chains. Practical implications For practitioners, the research highlights how HITL can be implemented to strengthen supply chain decision-making while ensuring compliance with ethical and regulatory standards. It suggests that organizations should prioritize training programs, design user-friendly interfaces and establish override mechanisms to maximize HITL effectiveness. The findings emphasize the importance of aligning AI investments with human oversight structures, rather than pursuing automation in isolation. Managers can use the framework to evaluate readiness, map decision tasks suitable for HITL integration and design workflows that balance speed, transparency and accountability. Social implications By positioning humans as active collaborators, HITL contributes to responsible AI adoption that safeguards jobs, reinforces accountability and reduces risks of algorithmic bias in supply chain operations. The approach ensures that technology complements rather than replaces human expertise, fostering inclusive digital transformation. From a societal perspective, embedding ethical safeguards into AI decision-making promotes trust in enterprise systems and enhances their legitimacy. The findings encourage the development of AI solutions that not only drive operational efficiency but also align with broader social values of fairness, responsibility and human dignity. Originality/value This research conceptualizes HITL as a dynamic socio-technical arrangement rather than a static control mechanism. The proposed AOA explains how human authority, algorithmic decision-making and organizational governance interact through oversight, trust calibration and distributed accountability, providing a mechanism-based conceptualization of HITL for OSCM.

items.title: Human–AI Collaboration in Higher Education: Faculty Readiness and Institutional Transformation—A Semantic Review and Bibliometric Mapping
items.abstract: Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is changing how academic work is planned, produced, assessed, communicated, and governed. Yet adoption is uneven: individual faculty members may experiment with AI while institutional workload models, assessment systems, professional development, and governance remain largely unchanged. This paper examines how human–AI collaboration, faculty readiness, and institutional change interact in higher education. Drawing on a semantic synthesis of literature already cited in the supplied data, the paper organises relevant work around five connected themes: AI literacy and faculty capability; task-level human–AI collaboration; professional identity and trust; organisational culture and change capability; and responsible governance. It proposes a transparent protocol for future bibliometric mapping. Importantly, this is a conceptual semantic review, not a completed database-based bibliometric study: no publication counts, co-citation networks, or keyword frequencies are reported as empirical findings. The synthesis suggests that faculty readiness is multidimensional and cannot be reduced to tool familiarity. It includes pedagogical judgement, critical evaluation of AI outputs, ethical awareness, disciplinary adaptation, and confidence to disclose and contest AI-supported decisions. Institutional change requires leadership, protected development time, policy clarity, peer learning, workload recognition, assessment redesign, and participatory governance. A conceptual framework links institutional conditions to faculty readiness, the quality of human–AI collaboration, and feedback into organisational strategy. The paper offers a practical readiness matrix and implementation pathway for higher education institutions, including Indian institutions navigating digital transformation. items.abstract: Hybrid Intelligence for Industrial Process Optimization: Establishing the Need Presentation delivered at the 23rd International Conference on Informatics in Control, Automation and Robotics (ICINCO 2026) within the Special Session on Hybrid Artificial Intelligence (HybAI 2026) held in Angers, France, October 26–28, 2026. Summary:Over 80% of industrial artificial intelligence proofs-of-concept (PoCs) stall or fail to reach production due to a fundamental structural mismatch: physical plants operate under rigorous thermodynamic and hydraulic conservation laws with zero fault tolerance, whereas pure data-driven machine learning models act as unconstrained black boxes omitting causal mechanisms. This presentation opens the HybAI 2026 Special Session by surveying the theoretical and practical imperatives for Hybrid Intelligence: Limits of Pure Data-Driven AI: Why the No Free Lunch theorem and severe physical exploration budgets make learning physics ab initio sample-inefficient and hazardous in production. Critique of Sutton's "Bitter Lesson": In digital games, simulation and trial-and-error exploration are computationally free; in municipal water systems and heavy industry, unconstrained exploration destroys hardware (pipe bursts, pump cavitation). Physical invariants are indispensable inductive scaffolds, not bottlenecks. Lessons from Neurorobotics: How biological motor control decomposes known morphological kinematics from state-dependent disturbance estimation, providing a direct design template for industrial gray-box digital twins. Acausal Physics & Differentiable SciML: Unifying Differential-Algebraic Equations (DAEs) with adjoint sensitivity analysis to guarantee safety and sample efficiency by design. items.title: iHELP: Intelligent Holistic Emergency Logistics Platform. A Cloud-Based Simulation-Optimization Platform for Disaster Logistics and Real-Time Situational Awareness
items.abstract: Natural disasters increasingly cause severe casualties, displacement, and economic destruction, yet emergency response operations are routinely hindered by fragmented inter-agency coordination, resource planning bottlenecks, and information limited to overwhelmed traditional communication channels. To address these operational challenges, this chapter presents the Intelligent Holistic Emergency Logistics Platform (iHELP), a cloud-based simulation-optimization system designed to coordinate multi-modal supply chains and provide real-time situational awareness during emergencies. Abstracting the challenge as a multi-commodity, multi-mode transportation problem, iHELP models the assignment, routing, and scheduling of heterogeneous vehicle fleets across ground, air, and maritime networks under dynamic operational constraints. To overcome data scarcity during emergencies, iHELP incorporates a dedicated Social Media Analytics Module that uses natural language processing, computer vision, and spatial clustering to ingest user posts, filter misinformation, compute confidence metrics, and infer urgent humanitarian needs. Additional integrated modules manage weather disruptions, service prioritization, and infrastructure availability. Decision-makers interact with the system via a web dashboard that visualizes animated operations, transporter utilization, and inventory trends. Developed and validated in collaboration with NATO’s Crisis Management and Disaster Response Center of Excellence through simulated flood response scenarios, iHELP demonstrates strong capability in delivering robust, high-quality emergency logistics plans under stress and uncertainty.

items.title: Impacts of generative AI skill development on academic adaptation and learning outcomes among university students
items.abstract: Understanding how university students perceive the development of their generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) skills over time can clarify how GenAI use relates to learning and academic outcomes. This study examined perceived skill-development trajectories, changes in learning practices, and associated academic gains using a retrospective questionnaire with 313 analyzed responses and interviews with 18 students across subject areas. Descriptive and comparative analyses and exploratory structural equation modeling (SEM) were integrated with thematic analysis. Perceived developmental trajectories were heterogeneous: 34.2% of students reported rapid early improvement followed by a plateau, 28.4% steady improvement, and 21.1% delayed acceleration. Development was also uneven across skills, with improvement in evaluating GenAI outputs perceived as more challenging; assignments were the most frequently selected driver of skill growth. Interviews further indicated increasingly specific prompting, tailored verification, and selective delegation, although some students reported stable routines, dependence, skipped reasoning, or improvements attributable partly to better GenAI tools. Academic gains were reported more often for assignments than for examinations. The SEM indicated a positive indirect association between perceived skill growth and academic gains through adaptation of assignment processes, whereas academic gains did not clearly differ across developmental trajectory groups after multiplicity correction. The findings suggest that perceived GenAI skill development varies in both trajectory and skill domain and is associated with changes in learning practices and differentiated academic benefits.

items.title: Implementing AI-Assisted Diabetic Retinopathy Screening: A Qualitative Evidence Synthesis of Data Governance, Trust and Equity
items.abstract: Diabetic retinopathy can be screened (assisted by artificial intelligence) in primary care and underserved contexts, and technical accuracy is irrelevant to whether patients and practitioners consider the service a legitimate offer.This secondary qualitative research study explored how trust, data ownership and equity are formed in empirical descriptions of AI-assisted retinal screening.A systematic search found 35 sources from 2016-2026.The findings were based on sixteen major articles published since 2021, whereas a different body informed the introduction, theoretical framework, research gap, methods and discussion of literature.This yielded three themes suggested by reflexive thematic synthesis: trust as a relational goal and not an assurance of accuracy alone; retinal data ownership is an open relationship of governance; equity is a dilemma of increased access and risk redistribution.Speed, convenience, and instant outcomes were well-regarded by patients, although this consideration faded as AI seemed to substitute clinical elucidation or reuse of data was opaque.Practitioners were open to AI when accountability, escalation channels, and training could be perceived, but raised anxieties over consent, accountability, information security, and skewed model performance.The greatest gains in access were most effective when AI was integrated within attainable care pathways, though inaccessible images, referral failure, digital savvy, and subgroup bias could recreate disparity.The paper finds that reliable AI eye screening entails human-controllable communication, purpose-driven data stewardship, and equity considerations throughout the screening process, not just at the algorithmic endpoint.The analytic focus is therefore multi-actor and system-level, integrating patient experience with practitioner readiness, institutional accountability, data governance and referral capacity.

items.abstract: This study proposes an organizational and economic framework for improving ERP-based integrated management in industrial enterprises, with particular emphasis on Uzbekistan's machinery manufacturing sector. It examines opportunities to enhance the integration of information systems, strengthen coordination among procurement, warehousing, and production operations, and improve the adaptability of conventional static inventory management policies. The proposed framework combines the integration of existing Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) functions, multi-model bills of materials (BOMs), feedback from Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES), dynamic calculations of safety stock and reorder points, and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted decision support under human supervision. An economic optimization model incorporates inventory holding costs, procurement costs, material shortage costs, and costs associated with production interruptions. Static and dynamic inventory management policies are compared using operational and economic performance indicators. The study presents a conceptual framework and an analytical evaluation methodology; empirical validation at the enterprise level requires actual production, inventory, and procurement data.

items.title: Improving Patient-Reported Understanding of Radiographic Reports in Spine Surgery Through Implementation of Natural Language Processing: A Randomized Controlled Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Many spinal imaging reports are written above recommended health literacy levels, limiting patient comprehension at a time when rapid electronic access to radiology results is increasing. We aim to evaluate whether supplemental natural language processing (NLP)–modified radiology reports—within the context of usual patient portal access to the original report—are associated with improved patient-reported perceived understandability compared with standard reports among patients undergoing spine imaging. METHODS: This is a prospective randomized controlled study with limited participant blinding, conducted with 2 spine surgeons affiliated with a single academic medical center in New York City. Participants (18 years or older) undergoing spine imaging at initial surgical consultation were enrolled and were randomized to receive either their original radiology report or a supplemental NLP–modified version. Radiology reports were rewritten using a standardized natural language processing prompt (ChatGPT 4.0) and reviewed for accuracy by study investigators. The primary outcome was survey-based patient-reported perceived understandability. Secondary outcomes included objective readability scores (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, Flesch Reading Ease, Simple Measure of Gobbledygook, Gunning-Fog Index). RESULTS: Fifty-two adults were enrolled; 42 (81%) completed the postintervention survey. Among 52 randomized participants (26 women [50%]), NLP–modified reports demonstrated significantly improved objective readability across all indices compared with original reports (Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, 5.9 ± 1.1 vs 11.0 ± 1.7; Reading Ease, 71.0 ± 10.3 vs 28.2 ± 12.5; Simple Measure of Gobbledygook, 20.1 ± 12.7 vs 23.5 ± 15.7; Gunning-Fog Index, 8.2 ± 1.1 vs 14.3 ± 1.8; all P < .01). Of 42 survey respondents, those receiving supplemental NLP-modified reports reported greater ease of understanding the report language (4.2 ± 1.2 vs 2.6 ± 1.5, mean-difference 95% CI: 0.75-2.53, P < .01, Bonferroni-corrected- P = .02), and less difficulty with medical terms (2.0 ± 1.5 vs 3.6 ± 1.4, mean-difference 95% CI: −2.51 to −0.60, P < .01, Bonferroni-corrected- P = .04). CONCLUSION: Supplemental NLP-modified radiology reports were associated with improved objective readability and higher patient-reported perceived ease of understanding in a spine surgery initial consultation setting. These findings support further investigation of NLP-generated supplemental explanations within supervised clinical workflows.

items.title: In-Browser Human-AI Co-Writing for Counterspeech: An Exploratory User Study of Agency, Perceived Response Quality, and Time
items.abstract: Writing counterspeech that challenges online hate speech can be cognitively and emotionally demanding, whereas fully automated generation may weaken users' sense of voice and responsibility. We present an in-browser AI-assisted co-writing tool that enables users to contribute their own ideas and offers three editable suggestions generated by a large language model using dynamically retrieved hate speech-counterspeech examples from the Multitarget CONAN dataset. We evaluated the tool in an exploratory within-subject study with ten participants, complemented by think-aloud observations and semi-structured interviews with half of the participants. Participants wrote responses to three self-selected hate speech instances without assistance and then repeated the task with the tool. Final responses were subsequently peer-rated for empathy, non-toxicity, relevance, specificity, and persuasiveness. Participants evaluated the interface positively, and qualitative accounts linked user input, selection among alternatives, and small edits to perceived agency and responsibility. Assisted responses received higher descriptive mean ratings across all five proxies, with the largest difference for empathy. Mean composition time increased from 2.52 to 3.88 minutes. Qualitative findings further revealed a tension between empathy-oriented outputs and users' desire to express legitimate anger or direct disagreement. We contribute exploratory design guidance for treating AI-assisted counterspeech as deliberative co-writing rather than automated text production.

items.title: Individual Characteristics, Job Characteristics, and Job Placement on Employee Performance at the Election Supervisory Agency of West Sulawesi Province
items.abstract: This study aims to examine and analyze the effects of individual characteristics, job characteristics, and job placement on employee performance at the Election Supervisory Agency (Bawaslu) of West Sulawesi Province, both individually and simultaneously. The study employs a quantitative method with an associative research approach. The population consists of 43 employees, all of whom were included as respondents using a saturated sampling technique. Data were collected through questionnaires, observations, interviews, and documentation. Instrument quality was assessed through validity and reliability tests, while the data were analyzed using classical assumption tests and multiple linear regression analysis with the assistance of SPSS software. Hypotheses were tested using t-tests, an F-test, and the coefficient of determination. The findings indicate that (1) individual characteristics have a positive and statistically significant effect on employee performance; (2) job characteristics have a positive and statistically significant effect on employee performance; (3) job placement has a positive and statistically significant effect on employee performance; and (4) individual characteristics, job characteristics, and job placement jointly have a statistically significant effect on employee performance. Individual characteristics emerged as the strongest predictor, with a standardized beta coefficient of 0.626. The adjusted R-squared value of 0.753 indicates that the three independent variables collectively explain approximately 75.3% of the variation in employee performance, while the remaining variation is not explained by the model. These findings highlight the importance of employee competencies, effective job design, and appropriate job placement in improving employee performance within public sector institutions.

items.title: IndoNutriQA: An Indonesian Clinical Nutrition Question Answering Benchmark
items.abstract: Clinical Question Answering (QA) underpins Clinical Intelligent Decision Support Systems, but progress is severely limited for low-resource languages such as Indonesian by the absence of public domain-specific data. We introduce IndoNutriQA, an expert-curated Indonesian clinical QA benchmark of 911 question-answer pairs built from real clinical-nutrition reports. Rather than a large-scale training corpus, it is positioned as a high-quality evaluation resource: every pair is grounded in a clinically relevant context, enriched with structured metadata (anthropometric assessment, medical diagnosis, document provenance, chunk segmentation). Eight standardised question types following the Nutrition Care Process (NCP), including the Problem, Etiology, Sign and Symptom (PES) diagnosis statement, are answered for every report, which was written by a graduate-level dietetic intern, by one of three nutritionists. Answers are free-form clinical prose rather than extractive spans, and an expert validation study finds 6-10% of reference answers contestable. The dataset supports generative, extractive and retrieval-augmented QA as well as zero- and few-shot LLM evaluation. We report fine-tuned baselines (IndoBERT variants, mT5, RAG) with 5-fold cross-validation, learning curves and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, and benchmark eight contemporary LLMs zero- and five-shot. We further calibrate our LLM-as-judge rubric against three expert raters (one RD, two nutritionists), finding it human-comparable on factuality and completeness but unreliable on clinical safety, and a human error analysis shows it misses unsupported content that the raters identify. IndoNutriQA is released to foster research in Indonesian clinical NLP and nutritional decision support.

items.title: Industrıal Applıcatıons of Artıfıcıal Intellıgence
items.abstract: In modern times, artificial intelligence (AI) is considered one of the most important technological revolutions in the industrialization process. Artificial Intelligence technologies are widely used to digitize, automate, and increase the efficiency of production. The basis of the “Industry 4.0” concept is precisely artificial intelligence, big data, robotics, and internet technologies. In this regard, studying the applications of Artificial Intelligence in the industrial field is relevant both theoretically and practically. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming various industries by providing new solutions, increasing efficiency, and reducing costs. Artificial Intelligence (AI) refers to the development of computer systems that can perform tasks that typically require human intelligence, such as learning, problem solving, perception, decision making, and language understanding. Artificial Intelligence systems use various techniques such as machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and computer vision to analyze large amounts of data and make predictions or decisions based on that analysis. Some examples of AI applications include virtual personal assistants, self-driving cars, image and speech recognition, and medical diagnostics and treatment. AI is a rapidly developing field and can transform many industries and aspects of daily life. Applications of AI in the industrial field are accompanied by automation of production, energy saving, increased safety, and the creation of new technological capabilities. In the future, the competitiveness of industrial enterprises will be measured precisely by the level of use of AI technologies.
